headlineHtml: Volumes confirmed, prices whipsawed: record TSMC revenue and power-equipment orders met a CEO shock at Nvidia and a hot PPI print

keyData.label: Next week
keyData.value: JP GDP 16 Nov / Nvidia 17 Nov / FOMC minutes 18 Nov

ledeHtml: This week's prints confirmed AI data-centre demand in volume terms across chips, servers, power equipment and machine tools. Prices told a different story: Nvidia lost its founder-CEO mid-week and US producer prices rose at the fastest annual pace since November 2022, unwinding the early-week semiconductor rotation by Friday.

bullets.html: TSMC's October revenue was a record NT$586.89bn (+59.7% YoY); Hon Hai's Q3 net profit was a record NT$77.5bn (+34%) with AI servers at 54% of sales; Applied Materials' Q4 revenue was a record (+53% YoY) and Cisco's Q1 revenue a record (+24%) with FY27 guidance raised.

bullets.leadHtml: Nvidia was the week's price event.
bullets.html: Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO and director with immediate effect (announced 12 Nov); CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The shares opened -13.1% on 12 Nov, recovered to close -4.34%, then fell a further 2.0% on 13 Nov to $162.85, below a $4tn market cap.

bullets.leadHtml: Power and machinery breadth was the second story.
bullets.html: Siemens' Q4 orders rose 58% to a record €34.77bn; Hitachi Energy India's orders rose 85.9% with a record backlog of ₹333.35bn and data centres its No. 2 order source; Japan's machine-tool orders hit an annual record in ten months; India approved its first 1,150 kV transmission project.
US October CPI came in hot (+0.4% MoM vs +0.3% consensus) and PPI rose +6.5% YoY, the largest since November 2022. Friday's US close unwound the rotation: Nasdaq -0.91%, SOX -3.4%, AMD -8.8%.

bullets.leadHtml: Capex and supply chains are still tightening.
bullets.html: Nebius raised 2026 capex guidance to about $27bn; CoreWeave's backlog reached $132.5bn; SMIC's utilisation was 97.3%; Samsung pulled its HBM packaging plant forward a year to June 2028; China's domestic AI accelerators' combined share passed Nvidia's for the first time (Huawei Ascend 28%).

blocks.heading: The week in numbers — rotation, then unwind
blocks.html:
The week had two halves. Into Wednesday, semiconductor and AI names were bought: on 11 Nov (US) the SOX rose 5.66% with all 30 constituents up, and CoreWeave gained 24.71% after its print. Tokyo did not follow on 12 Nov — the Nikkei fell 0.70% to 60,819.36 on afternoon selling in chip and AI names (Advantest the largest drag) while TOPIX rose 0.20%, showing the selling was concentrated rather than broad.

By Friday the trade had reversed. The US close on 13 Nov was Nasdaq -0.91%, SOX -3.4%, AMD -8.8% and Nvidia -2.0%. Tokyo steadied the same day (Nikkei +0.53% to 61,142.35, TOPIX +0.11%). A full weekly sector matrix for the US, China, Taiwan, Korea and Europe is the standard pack from the next edition; in this test run, the Japan industry snapshot below is shown as the format sample, and weekly moves for the other regions are marked 未取得 rather than estimated.

blocks.heading: Sector and company performance — Japan snapshot
blocks.html:
TradingView's Japan industry table (latest session, retrieved 15 Nov) shows how uneven the Japan tape was beneath a flat index: electrical products fell 4.05% and communications equipment 2.36%, electronic components fell 1.66% and semiconductors 1.06%, while computer hardware rose 1.68% and electronic equipment & instruments rose 0.72%. Industrial machinery was roughly flat (+0.17%) and trucks/construction/agricultural machinery fell 1.17%.

Company-level, the week's defining path was Nvidia's (Figure 3): a -13.1% open on the resignation, a recovery to -4.34% by that close, and a further slide to $162.85 on 13 Nov. The pattern — an idiosyncratic governance shock, rotation into AMD and Broadcom early in the week, then a sector-wide unwind on the PPI print — is the template the catalyst table in Part 3 works through event by event.

blocks.heading: Semiconductors and AIDC — the prints
blocks.html:
TSMC's October revenue of NT$586.89bn (+59.7% YoY) was its largest month on record, taking January–October revenue to NT$4,485.62bn (+43.3%). Applied Materials posted record Q4 revenue (+53% YoY) and Cisco record Q1 revenue (+24%) with FY27 guidance raised. In Japan, Japan Micronics' nine-month operating profit rose 138.9% YoY with guidance and the dividend raised, and Eblen's H1 operating profit rose 106% — evidence that HBM-related investment is reaching measurement and control equipment.

On the demand side, CoreWeave's Q3 revenue was $3.66bn (+168% YoY) with backlog of $132.5bn, but a net loss of $709M and interest expense of $846M; Nebius' Q3 revenue was $980.8M (+571%) while 2026 capex guidance rose to about $27bn and some third-party capacity slipped into H1 2027. Anthropic's Q3 compute and infrastructure spend was $9.9bn, 58% of its revenue. The constraint set — funding cost and delivery capacity, not end demand — is unchanged. Figure 2 puts the week's growth prints side by side.

blocks.heading: Power, machinery and factory automation
blocks.html:
Siemens' Q4 orders of €34.77bn (+58%) were a record, led by smart infrastructure including data-centre electrical equipment, and its medium-term growth target was raised. Hitachi Energy India's Q2 (Jul–Sep) orders rose 85.9% to ₹41.21bn on revenue of ₹29.97bn (+63.6%), with backlog at a record ₹333.35bn — roughly 11x one quarter's revenue. GE Vernova won 765 kV transformer orders (70+ units) from India's POWERGRID, and India approved its first 1,150 kV project (₹68,816 crore, about six years).

Japan's October machine-tool orders were ¥204.4bn (+42.5% YoY), breaking the annual record in ten months. Amada raised its FY net profit forecast to ¥40bn (+31%) on AI data-centre sheet-metal demand; SMC raised its full-year recurring profit forecast by 36.0% with a buyback of up to ¥50bn; THK raised its net profit forecast to ¥58.8bn; Takasago Thermal raised its operating profit forecast 20% to ¥60bn with an orders forecast of ¥620bn for the first time. On 14 Nov, Infineon announced supply of the first 900V GaN bidirectional switch to Enphase for solid-state transformers — the power-semiconductor layer of the same AIDC power chain.

blocks.heading: Capex, trade and demand statistics
blocks.html:
The statistics tracker (Figure 5) is the fixed panel for this report: country capex, trade flows (imports, exports), shipments and demand indicators, read together rather than as isolated releases. This week it shows a consistent picture — US inflation sticky at the producer level, Chinese foundry utilisation at 97.3% (SMIC Q3 revenue a record $3.19bn), hyperscaler-linked capex guidance still rising (Nebius), and capacity being pulled forward where it is scarce (Samsung's HBM packaging plant, one year earlier to June 2028; investment amount 未取得).

GlobalFoundries' Q3 gross margin was a record 31.4% and its 2026 silicon-photonics outlook was raised to $500M — a data point for the optical/CPO theme that now sits in this report's coverage. ams OSRAM was the week's counter-example: Q3 sales of €829M and €3.8bn of cumulative design wins, but shares down 9.2% on disappointing Q4 guidance.

blocks.heading: Part 3 — Catalysts and the week ahead
Catalyst attribution — why it moved, why it happened
blocks.html: Figure 6 lists the events that actually drove the week's performance, with the mechanism in each case. Two patterns matter. First, the largest single-stock move (Nvidia) was a governance event, not a demand event — the announcement came because a board investigation into the founder's conduct left no alternative, and the price fell on succession uncertainty (no designated No. 2, a CFO as interim CEO) rather than on any change to orders or guidance. Second, the sector-level moves were expectation trades: hot CPI and PPI prints moved the discount rate, and the same names that had been bought on prints early in the week were sold on macro by Friday.

blocks.heading: Week ahead — 16 to 22 November
blocks.html: Monday 16 Nov: Japan's Q3 GDP first estimate — the split between domestic demand and capex is the read. Tuesday 17 Nov (US time; Wednesday morning JST): Nvidia's Q3 results — company guidance is revenue of $108bn ±2% against consensus of about $111.4bn; the form of guidance under the interim CEO and any comment on funding commitments matter as much as the print. Wednesday 18 Nov: FOMC minutes, and the requested closed-door congressional briefing on the Huang matter. Thursday 19 Nov: Japan's machinery orders. Each of these maps to a tracker in Figure 5; next week's edition will score them against the expectations recorded here.

blocks.heading: Idea candidates — for the reader's judgement
blocks.html: Candidates only; the analysis and any decision sit with the reader. (1) Power-equipment breadth: orders at Siemens, Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova, plus record Japan machine-tool orders, against share prices that sold off with the semiconductor complex on 13–14 Nov — variant perception to test: whether the market is pricing power equipment as a derivative of the chip trade rather than on its own backlog (about 2.8 years of revenue at Hitachi Energy India). Catalyst: Nvidia's print and any hyperscaler capex commentary. Kill condition: order cancellations or lead-time compression in the next prints. (2) Nvidia succession discount: the shares closed the week about 36% below the October high with demand indicators (TSMC, backlog data) still rising — the question is whether the discount is governance-only and therefore closable by a credible succession plan at the 17 Nov print. Risk: the congressional process on 18 Nov extends the overhang.
